records.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
records.author: kmansm27
records.storyText:
Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.

Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:

Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.

Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

The entire codebase is open source at https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara, and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at https://omnara.com. Let me know what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Stackdome – An open source self-hostable Railway alternative on K8s
records.author: basilpbabu
records.storyText:
Since Railway getting pwned is getting all the attention right now, I thought now is a good time to showcase what we've been building. Stackdome is a self hosted platform as a service. The idea is to have simplicity of platforms like Railway and Render, but with the ability to run everything on infrastructure you control.

With Stackdome, you can deploy an application from GitHub, connect multiple services visually, add a managed database, create preview environments, and roll back the entire application if a release breaks.

Features:

- First class support for multi-service applications, shown on a canvas in the UI (inspired by Railway). You can edit, wire up, and create resources from the canvas.

- First class support for multiple clusters. Stackdome acts as the hub and places workloads across clusters (hub and spoke).

- Self hostable, from a small VPS to a large k8s cluster.

- Managed Postgres with WAL archiving, HA, backups, and PITR (CNPG underneath).

- A release system for the whole stack. A release targets everything, and you can roll it back if something breaks.

- Source to image, with an in cluster registry (Zot).

- Disposable preview environments, which can also be multi-service.

- Declarative apps via a Stackfile, deployed with the CLI.

Basically, the idea is to package the tooling in the CNCF/cloud-native ecosystem into an opinionated platform, so that developers can get a without being an expert in Kubernetes or a dozen other projects from the CNCF landscape.

Docs: https://docs.stackdome.com

records.title: Show HN: Skillstore – Expert skills your coding agent fetches as it works
records.author: jkkorn
records.storyText:
TLDR: Connect once to your favorite coding agent. Claude Code and Codex find and load relevant skills for the task at hand, from expert developers or your own team.

Hey HN I was originally a bit frustrated with having to scour github repos for the right skill while I tried to improve an iOS app's Swift animation.

Then I got frustrated with having to force the agent to use the right skill for the right task.

So I built Skillstore: a library of engineering skills behind an MCP server. Claude Code and Codex can search it, load relevant instructions, and apply them to your task. You don’t need to know the skill’s name beforehand.

Skills are loaded on demand, so you don’t have to keep the whole library in your prompt. (ideally with help you also save tokens and preserve the context window)

ex: In our running app, a review using Paul Hudson’s SwiftUI skill caught undersized touch targets and controls that VoiceOver couldn’t meaningfully identify. We fixed those before the release. In our gym app, a Skillstore-guided review caught an onboarding layout overflowing on small iPhones at large text sizes.

You describe the work → your agent finds relevant expertise → your agent uses it.

You dont have to browse github repos and filter by stars anymore. And you dont have to invoke skills by name You can also give your team a shared library of private skills

Been using it inhouse and with friends for the past 2 months.

Favorite feature so far: Turning a tutorial into a private skill, so the agent can use that knowledge on future tasks when the time is right

You can try the public library without an account https://skillstore-jk.fly.dev/developers#try

Send me your feedback :)

records.title: Show HN: Overdesigned Simple Solitaire
records.author: fsloth
records.storyText:
I got irritated by the maximalism and lack of aesthetics present in modern software when trying to find a nice solitaire.

A solitaire does not need a score, levels - and most of all it does not need to download anything, have user log in or do anything else except maintain game state.

So since software comes automatically nowadays, I decided as a weekend project to create the last solitaire I'll ever need.

The application is built on Rust so I can compile it to native. But it runs just as well as web app!

I geeked out completely on design (it may look like "default" but that's the point) to create as non-intruding yet aesthetically pleasing experience as I could.

I might have accidentally put in a complete card design system with a content pipeline (maybe I'll do default blackjack next) - but as a player you only see the one pack of cards.

Anyway, hope someone here appreciates the minimalistic aesthetics.

The game state is saved in the url so if you want to save a nice game you can do it by copypasting the link.

The game engine is versioned so if I ever change the engine or state schema there will be support for the current version as well.

There _is_ a novelty.

If you click the "teach" button it shows all the available free moves as arrows.

Hope this is fun for someone!

records.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
records.author: dsmurrell
records.storyText:
I'm not a good singer, but strangely enough I still like singing. I've improved a little over time with singing apps, but their song lists are limited by licensing, so I'd often open a song expecting the original and find a cover I didn't want to sing to.

So I built OnKey: a free, open-source (MIT) Mac app that listens to whatever you're playing in Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube, learns the singer's melody, and shows you live where you're sharp or flat, with a score at the end. Nightingale did something similar years ago for your own audio files. OnKey works with the music you already stream.

Demo (1:35, sound on): https://singonkey.app

The first time you play a song, you can sing along while it listens, or play a whole playlist and let OnKey learn the songs in the background before you come back to sing them. When a song finishes it learns the notes on your Mac (a couple of minutes), and from the second play the notes scroll towards you before you sing them.

Learning the song and scoring you both happen on your Mac. No account, no analytics, and the music is never saved or sent anywhere. Your takes stay there too. To check the score means something, I ran 20 recordings of singers, from poor to professional, that music experts had already scored. OnKey ranked them in nearly the same order as the experts did.

It's still rough in places: busy mixes and harmonies can confuse which voice is the tune, and now and then a note lands an octave off. Scoring is forgiving on purpose for now, set for beginners like me, so stricter modes for better singers are next. And it's Apple Silicon and macOS 14.2+ only.

I'd love to hear where it scores you unfairly or the notes go wrong, and I'm happy to answer questions about how it hears the music and learns a song.

records.title: Show HN: PDT – Open-source deployment of scheduled jobs on your own cloud
records.author: visch
records.storyText:
Hi, I'm Derek. I've been doing data integrations / ETL work since 2014, first for K-12, now for commercial companies think ADP/BambooHR to AzureAD, etc. I've written so many deployment systems for integrations, each slightly different. Instead, we took the best parts of all the systems we've built and put them into one tool. PDT takes your job and deploys it to AWS, Azure, GCP, or even Task Scheduler. It's a convention-over-configuration deployment tool specifically made for Scheduled Jobs. Things like data integrations, scans, reports, etc.

With AI, writing scripts is easier than ever. Deploying them into production isn't as easy. Because the AI needs to know what you want, this can be tricky as there are so many choices to make! Do I use Azure Functions, Duarble Functions, Container Instances, Azure Batch, AKS CronJob, Azure Automation Runbooks, Logic Apps? ahhh, I just want this to run in production.

To give it a shot, install uv, then:

  uv tool install pdt-cli
  uv tool update-shell
  pdt init jobs
  cd jobs
  pdt run hello-world # runs locally
  pdt deploy hello-world # runs on cloud 
  pdt new hello --from powershell-hello-world # give powershell a shot
PDT gives you a standard set of primitives to use for scheduling, secrets, storage, logs, and alerts. This means you already know how to track state, where to drop the file you wanted to drop, how to know when the job fails, and how to answer all the other orchestration-related questions.

It's an asynchronous HTTP/HTTPS header inspection tool that fingerprints PHP and compares the version against the PHP2Shell fixed releases. Obviously this isn't a foolproof way of knowing if a host is vulnerable (See Security disclaimer in README.md), but it's at least good at finding hosts in your environment that are advertising to the internet that they are using a vulnerable version of PHP.

records.title: Show HN: Moin – A P2P voice app built on iroh and Media over QUIC
records.author: culinary-robot
records.storyText:
The first voice chat app I used with friends was Roger Wilco back in 1999. We later moved to TeamSpeak, Ventrilo and Mumble. I loved how simple and self-hostable they were. Then Discord came along...

With Moin, we wanted to bring some of that simplicity back. We focus on two things: low-latency voice chat and smooth 60 fps screen sharing. A modern take on the classics.

There is no account, no ads, no trackers or any sign-up. Open Moin, start your own Space (a server running locally inside the app), and invite friends with a link. For something more permanent, you can self-host a Community server or let us host it.

The UI is Flutter, while everything else is Rust, built using iroh and Media over QUIC. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, including screen sharing through an SFU, which only sees encrypted data.

records.title: Show HN: Embodsi – Embodied Super Intelligence
records.author: laser
records.storyText:
embodsi is a generative AI MMO experience that runs in the browser. It allows people to communicate (text, audio, video, avatar emotes and movement) and collaboratively build 3D spaces and games via LLMs connected to harnesses and sandboxes for object modeling, space layout, game logic, and driving persistent avatars with shared context and memory.

It’s different from existing 3D social apps (AFAIK) because it enables people to build multiplayer virtual worlds, games, and characters with generative AI right from their browser (desktop, mobile, or VR), in nearly infinitely-extendable recursively tiled interconnected spaces, while allowing people to interact in a public commons or easily create a private channel to enjoy the same spaces with their chosen friends and community.

The brief backstory is I was running my personal “pelican benchmark” [1] on GPT-6 Astra, which when I ran on Gemini 3 Pro last November couldn’t even put heads on 3D models the right side up [2], and was astounded by the initial results. I gained inspiration for an art project and social experiment that was going to have nine interconnected, benevolent virtual worlds that people could explore and hang out in with AI characters, but by the time Opus 5.5 was released I was gaining so much momentum and having so many ideas and so much fun building I just kept building more and more with the constraint of minimizing MVP scope lifted by agentic coding. I let the project become an ever-evolving wishlist of capabilities for a more interesting social environment as I became increasingly fascinated with the prospect of embodying creative machine intelligence in 3D space with people, realizing that rather than just limiting to building the spaces and characters I imagined I might enable people to co-create endless spaces and characters in a shared world.

There’s so much to do still but I’m sharing now even if it feels a little too soon (this is the first public announcement of embodsi’s existence) because I think it’s better to build in the open so people might guide the development and help it evolve in a good direction as model capability improves at a jaw-dropping pace.

For people that have the budget to build I hope to see you in embodsi creating amazing things! And for everyone regardless of means (I’ve tried to keep as much free and accessible as financially feasible) I hope you meet amazing people, discover awesome spaces, and enjoy your time in embodsi :)

I’ll be around here and embodsi to answer any questions! Thanks for your feedback and critique.

- Laser

P.S. SI != AI — but an emergent property of many people and what we create cascading and recursively interacting [3]

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50074156

[2] https://x.com/lasernite/status/1991021951301923107

[3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaia_hypothesis

records.title: Show HN: ReviewerAgent and StopContinue, for CC and Codex with Pi
records.author: raylad
records.storyText:
This package is designed to solve two problems:

1. Frontier models like Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Astra 6.0 and Sol 6.1 all make errors and bugs that can be found by another model (even a much smaller model like Luna).

2. In what is supposed to be a long development run, for example against a plan, models will decide to stop before they are finished, when there is obviously more work to do, or to ask a question they already should know the answer to.

ReviewerAgent blocks git commits and sends them to another agent that reviews the staged files and either allows the commit or returns a list of issues to fix.

StopContinue evaluates every agent stop and determines if it still has work to do or if it is asking a question that it has the answer to already. In either of those cases, it prompts the agent to keep working and specifies next steps or answers to questions, based on the current plan document and chat history.

The system works for and is tested on Claude Code and Codex as the developer harness, and either of those or any other model, through Pi, as the reviewer.

I've developed it over the last 4 months or so and used it daily over that period.

Take a look if it sounds useful. It's been tested on MacOS and Linux (Ubuntu), and has agent assisted install, update, and removal scripts, for convenience.

Stats:

Over four months of daily use of the system while developing it (from late June til today), reviewerAgent (usually a GPT Luna model) gated 3,877 commits, running about 7,600 reviews in total, so about half of those commits were rejected at least once.

The coding agent (Fable or Opus) almost never disagreed with the reviewer's judgements: over the last month, for example, it pushed back on just 3 of 693 rejections.

Each rejection listed an average of two required fixes and most rejected commits were accepted after a second round (90% within five attempts).

Rejection rates increased with commit size: only 23% of code commits under 50 lines were sent back, but 72% of those over 1,000 lines were initially rejected.

Here's an example of a bug that it caught last month for me. More examples in the README:

The Fable 5.1 developer agent wrote a wrapper script that runs a set of R validation checks against a freshly loaded database and records whether each one passed. (One of two required fixes shown.)

REQUIRED FIXES (blocking)

  2.  docs/database-phase-loader/local-load/run_r_checks.sh:4-6 pipes each R check through
      tail without pipefail or explicit status handling, so a failed Rscript can still
      produce a zero exit status and be recorded as successful. Preserve and propagate each
      check's exit status.
In a shell pipeline the exit status is that of the last command, so `Rscript check.R | tail` reports `tail`'s success even when the check fails. The script prints the tail of the failing check's output, exits 0, and records a pass. A broken load would have been certified as validated.

records.title: Show HN: A fantasy map of my blog to replace the chronological feed
records.author: mrcgnc
records.storyText:
This is my blog drawn as a network, with a light coat of paint to make it look like a video game map. Each city is a post, bigger cities have more incoming links, and roads are connections between posts. It updates semi-automatically every time I publish. (I used an LLM to write the code and drew about 90% of the art myself in Inkscape.)

For a long time I've been unsatisfied with the linear feeds and tag soups that most blogs use, so I decided to experiment with a non-linear view. I built some CLI tools that combine embedding similarity, LLM suggestions and human review to find the links between posts and quantify their strength. Now, every time I write a new piece, it takes me about 5 minutes to generate its links to/from older posts and grow the map accordingly.

The map is meant to look playful more than precise. For me, the key feature is how it enables making your own "journey" through the blog. The tricky part was finding a layout where closely related posts end up near each other AND the landscape doesn't change dramatically with every new post. I'm not a graph expert, but t-SNE on shortest-path distances over the link graph turned out to work well in my tests. Each update starts from the previous positions with early exaggeration off, and a Procrustes alignment keeps the map from rotating or drifting.

I hope it helps people get lost in there and find things they want to read. I'd like to see something like this on other blogs, so I'm sharing it here. I wonder if anyone else has tried similar ways to un-linearize their blogs.

records.title: Show HN: Is there a YC advantage for sales?
records.author: 30minAdayHN
records.storyText:
Hi all,

I had a hypothesis that YC companies sell to other YC companies. Many times to their own batch, other times to older YC companies. One of my YC friends told me that when they approached a big, well-known company for a potential pilot, the director of engineering there was a YC alum. He said "yeah, I understand" and gave them a pilot or LOI.

My theory is that most of the logos YC startups show on their landing pages will be other YC companies. They'll use that momentum at Demo Day to raise their seed round. What this also means is that sometimes, when I read Launch HNs or look at other YC products, I get the perception that they're very mature products (kudos to their design), and often that perception comes from the logos. So as someone looking to buy a YC product, I'm not sure if I'm being hustled or if they actually have a good customer base.

I'm not judging them. This is genuine curiosity, and also, this is what the YC advantage means. I set out to test my hypothesis by running my agents against YC's Summer 2026 batch: visit each landing page, look for customer logos, and check what percent of those are YC companies.

What do I get out of this? Probably nothing :p Just curious.

Here's a quick summary: - My hypothesis that most logos will be other YC companies is wrong. - In certain sub segments like horizontal AI tools, I did see that ~40% logos are YC companies.

Check the link for the analysis. Curious what your thoughts are? Any other directions we can push the analysis into?

records.title: Show HN: IDE for a general-purpose visual programming language "Pipe"
records.author: toplinesoftsys
records.storyText:
I'm happy to announce the release of the web-based Pipe IDE, availablle by clicking button "Try Pipe IDE" on website.

Pipe IDE requires no account - all data is stored locally in your browser's database, keeping friction to a minimum.

======

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why now?

The need for visual programming has become especially clear now that we're building with AI, which has introduced several serious problems that appear unrelated - yet visual programming addresses all of them at the root:

- AI predictability and customization. Instead of relying on one unpredictable, hard-to-customize model - which can only be changed through costly, time-consuming retraining - you can split it into small, specialized, and therefore more predictable agents, then build an explicitly programmed orchestration layer on top to coordinate them. Customization then happens through that orchestration layer, and visual programming is a far more user-friendly way to do it. This shift is already underway - specialized models like TypeSafe's Jev are built for exactly this kind of orchestration.

- Cybersecurity. AI makes it far easier for anyone to find and exploit vulnerabilities, so threats are growing. Because Pipe is semantically powerful enough to keep the entire program as a live visual graph in production rather than compiling it into a single opaque artifact, every block in an application stays directly accessible. That access solves two long-standing problems at once: slow patching, by swapping, disabling, or rerouting a faulty block in place instead of waiting on a full CI/CD deployment; and partially-blind monitoring, by tapping the inputs and outputs of any or all blocks directly, so telemetry no longer depends on log statements that may be missing where you need them.The EU Cyber Resilience Act's core demands map directly onto these capabilities - independent confirmation this approach is where regulation is heading.

- Code review. AI writes code faster than developers can review it, and leaning on AI to review AI doesn't fix the root problem - that AI can hallucinate too, so human eyes are still required. Visual programming gives those eyes a far clearer representation of the logic to review. AI-introduced errors are already piling up in production code - one study found nearly a quarter survive for months as silent technical debt.

2. Why start with a book instead of building the software first?

Most new languages start with an implementation. For visual languages, that software-first path is exactly what traps them in a single domain and keeps them from ever becoming general-purpose. I did the opposite and specified the full language first; the software is what I'm actively building now.

It avoids both failure modes. Software-first visual languages get stuck in their first implementation's domain, while purely theoretical ones get buried in complexity - too intricate and incomplete to be practical. Pipe takes the middle ground: well-chosen, practical primitives within a complete, coherent architecture.

The book's subtitle says it best - "A Pragmatic Approach to Visual Programming." It rests on seven years of R&D but stays in the practical lane, and the result is a consistent, usable, end-to-end visual language.

3. Do we need to rewrite our existing system in Pipe?

To some extent, yes - but the transition is far less disruptive than it sounds:

- The migration is gradual - you don't have to discard all existing code at once. You start by wrapping your entire project in a single top-level block. That's the initial step. Then, whenever you're ready, you add a workflow inside that top-level block and distribute the code across the visual blocks of the newly created workflow - and you can keep going, level by level.

- You choose how far to go. You can stop subdividing blocks at any point, so it's entirely your decision which parts of the system become visual and which remain as text.

- Pipe makes integration easy. It provides a simple bridge for connecting visual blocks to your existing text code.

- AI reduces the overhead of going visual. AI can generate diagram layouts from your existing code, update them as the code changes, suggest how to partition logic across blocks, and flag structural issues as your model grows.

4. We tried visual programming before, and it didn't work.

Every technology advances in a spiral - it fails several times before its lessons are learned and it finally succeeds. Pipe was built by studying exactly why earlier visual languages fell short. Two lessons in particular shaped it:

- A visual language must be both general-purpose and semantically powerful to compete with text. Text-based languages dominate precisely because they have both qualities; any visual language that lacks either will fail. Pipe has both.

- The answer isn't to swing between extremes. We tried pure visual programming, it didn't work, so we went back to text-only - which has its own problems, now made obvious by AI. Good engineering doesn't jump between extremes; it finds a synthesis that keeps the strengths of each while minimizing their weaknesses. That's Pipe's core philosophy: it doesn't replace text-based languages - it complements them. In practice, that means the developer decides what goes into visual diagrams and what stays as text.

records.storyText:
Yo party people!

The Electronic DJ Model (EDM) is an transformer model trained from scratch that generates a DJ playlist track-by-track curated to your initial track selection. It learned from nearly 5,000 real DJ sets in the DJ Mix Dataset.

The Idea: A DJ mix is an ordered list of music tracks, similar to how a sentence is an ordered list of words. We developed a novel tokenizer to handle the 63,040 unique tracks in the DJ Mix Dataset.

Limitations: With only ~96K tracks of training data, the big models memorized mixes. A small ~8M-parameter model did best: it learned patterns instead of copying them.

Continuous Improvement: Press thumbs-up to give positive feedback. Press thumbs-down to replace with a new track. Preferences are anonymously captured for DPO improvement to the model

Despite these limitations, I have enjoyed listening to the generated DJ sets. How was your personalized DJ set?

records.title: Show HN: Replacing CAPTCHAs with adaptive proof-of-work in WordPress
records.author: MatthiasNordwig
records.storyText:
I built this WordPress plugin because I was tired of the usual spam-protection tradeoff:

annoy users with CAPTCHAs, or send visitor data to a third-party service. This plugin uses a small proof-of-work challenge that runs in the browser before a form submission is accepted. Legitimate users normally don't have to solve anything, but large-scale automated spam becomes more expensive. A few implementation details:

Everything runs on the site's own server. There is no external service, API, or reputation system involved. The plugin doesn't set its own cookies. It only reads the standard WordPress login cookie to identify logged-in users. Form submissions are detected from the incoming request itself rather than through per-builder integrations. The client-side script is about 14 KB compressed. The project is GPL-2.0 licensed, has been available since November 2022, and currently has 4,000+ active installations. One thing people often ask about: the plugin ships with detection patterns for 80+ popular form builders. These are configuration patterns rather than dedicated integration code. The goal is to avoid maintaining custom implementations for every builder. The proof-of-work difficulty is adaptive. During spam waves the challenge becomes harder, which makes submissions a bit slower for everyone, but mostly increases the cost for bulk senders. Each difficulty level roughly doubles the required work. If you'd like to test it, there's a Live Preview on the WordPress.org plugin page, so you can try it directly in your browser without installing anything. Happy to answer questions about the proof-of-work approach, form detection, privacy implications, and tradeoffs.

records.author: aubryio
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I'm Aubry, a software engineer from Switzerland working in the mobility industry. In my spare time I've been building https://isochrone.ch, an interactive map that shows where you can go by public transport from any location in Switzerland.

The idea came from a simple frustration: traditional journey planners are great when you already know where you want to go, but what if you don't? For example, where could I go hiking within 90 minutes of Lausanne? Or which towns could I live in while keeping my commute under 45 minutes?

The interesting part was making this truly interactive. Public transport routing involves large timetables and most solutions rely on server-side routing which introduces latency every time you change something. I wanted to see if I could do the whole routing directly in the browser which led me to develop Minotor (https://minotor.dev), an open-source transit routing library using a compact in-memory representation of the timetable data and implements the RAPTOR routing algorithm. Once the data is loaded, routing calculations happen entirely client-side, making it superfast.

The project uses Swiss open public transport data from https://opentransportdata.swiss.

I first released it early 2025 and have been improving it since. It's completely free with no registration required.

I'd be curious to hear your thoughts :)

records.storyText:
I was looking at GLP-1 explanations on the web (full disclosure is that I founded a GLP-1 tracker dashboard) and saw that many had standard text, along with illustrations showing arrows pointing from GLP-1 to a bunch of organs. I didn’t think those sites were particularly memorable or helpful in understanding the actions and side effects. I’m an MD + computer science hybrid with a background in building interactive tools for helping people understand medical concepts, so I decided to build a free scroll-through explainer in the form of a subway ride. The ride is 7 stops, takes about 5-10 minutes, and doesn’t require an account.

This was with the assistance of AI, using multiple tools. The process was far from one-shot and with me heavily in the loop for all the different pieces. I still find it tricky to get something medically accurate and useful when the details matter. I had built a free set of pages, GLP-1 Field Guides, to help people understand the different GLP-1 related drug classes, and I was able to lean on all of that research and sources to get the details right and to provide authoritative sources for the information presented at each subway stop.

I had tried building this starting in February but then paused it for a few months because the models weren’t quite at the point where I could make what I had in my mind’s eye. In the final piece, the different animated elements are drawn in code and change with the scrolling. Here are some of the tools I ended up using:

- GPT Image and Nano Banana, both via a custom Claude Code skill I wrote, with my own sketches as the base, for the Field Guide visuals that were important for this piece. Nano Banana for the subway graffiti and the organs

- Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS for the conductor’s voice

- Suno for the song (ride to the end)

- Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to build the site and Codex for code review

I am curious if this is a useful format for understanding GLP-1s but happy to answer questions about any of the above.

records.title: Show HN: Caudra – An open-source terminal coding agent in one native binary
records.author: netsroht
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Thorsten. Caudra (https://caudra.ai) is an open source TUI coding agent written in Rust. It started as a fork of Maki and has grown into its own project.

I spend most of my working day with coding agents and i have tried a lot of them. I kept adding more and more plugins to get the features I wanted. Most of the time though, i couldn't build the plugins i needed because I couldn't hook into the places I needed (e.g. proper /goal mode). It was also hard to keep them up-to-date, and I wanted one binary I could install in new environments and use right away. It also had to work with small/fast (even local) models as well as flagship ones.

I'd like to have feedback on these things:

- Steering: You can send a message as "next" (after the turn ends), "guide" (at the next safe point) or "replace" (right now). IMO, "next" is useful for simple ad-hoc chains.

- /btw: Ask a side question while the main agent keeps working. It reuses the prompt cache, so follow-ups are cheap. This works even during an active question prompt.

- Small/fast models: Caudra nudges the model when a turn stalls, which helps models like Qwen3.8-27B that sometimes stop early.

The conversation is always append-only, so the provider cache stays warm. From using it myself, I see about 97% cache hits with anthropic models and 94% with openai.

It's still in preview. I'd like to hear what breaks and what you'd want before you'd consider to switch.

Repo: https://github.com/caudra/caudra

Clips: https://caudra.ai/gallery/

records.title: Show HN: Toli – Let Claude Code on one computer work with Codex on another
records.author: alama24
records.storyText:
A month or so ago, a colleague was running some code my team owned on his machine and hit a niche Windows kernel-related Python issue. We were debugging it together, but kept having to relay information between our coding agents, mine understood the codebase, while his had the context of the environment where it was actually failing.

At some point I realized we were basically acting as the message bus between them, copying findings and questions back and forth.

That made me wonder, why not just let the agents work together directly?

I found A2A and built toli, a local daemon that an existing agent can connect to over MCP, giving it the plumbing to discover and work with A2A peers, including another person’s toli-connected agent on another machine.

It also works locally. I use it to let two of my agents working on sister codebases collaborate on bugs and design without having to give either agent both repos.

Would love feedback:

https://github.com/arjunvlama/toli

records.title: Show HN: Bliss Writer – Screenwriting TUI Built with Roc
records.author: oDot
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I thought you may find my screenwriting software interesting, even if you aren't writing yourself.

It's built with Roc[0], a functional language compiling to machine code, where I/O is provided by a concept called "platforms".

Is Bliss Writer's case, the platform is in Rust, using Crossterm and bits of Ratatui.

This is all then packaged by Trolley[1], which ships bundles the TUI with Ghostty, similarly to how Electron bundles webapps with a browser.

It's pretty fast for a beta. You can use Ctrl+Shift+Alt+0 for an frame-time monitor

[0] https://www.roc-lang.org/ [1] https://github.com/weedonandscott/trolley

records.title: Show HN: MandarinClips 180k movie clips for teaching Chinese
records.author: mandarinclips
records.storyText:
I built MandarinClips (https://www.mandarinclips.com) – an audiovisual corpus of 180,000+ real film and drama dialogue clips for Chinese language teachers and learners.

### Why I Built This For language teachers, finding authentic real-world video materials for class is notoriously painful. Textbooks often provide rigid, robotic dialogues (e.g., "你好吗？我很好"), but native speakers use nuanced particles (吧, 呢, 嘛), colloquial phrasing, and messy natural rhythm.

I wanted to give Chinese educators and students an instant way to find authentic audiovisual examples instead of having to manually clip movies or invent artificial example sentences.

### What It Does - 180,000+ segmented Chinese cinema dialogue snippets with aligned subtitles. - Search by specific keywords, grammatical structures, or spoken patterns. - Instantly pull up short 3-10 second clips showing how different native speakers use a phrase across different emotional and situational contexts.

I would love to hear feedback from educators, language enthusiasts, or anyone learning Chinese on HN! What features would make this more useful for your teaching or studying?

records.title: Show HN: I built an app to stop doomscrolling while waiting for Codex to finish
records.author: juanferreras
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I usually have a couple of threads running on Codex, but some time ago I realized I was opening X or Instagram and doomscrolling while the agents did the work. I went from regularly getting into a flow state while coding manually to almost the complete opposite. Basically speedrunning a shorter attention span.

A friend and I built LightScroll partly to help with this. It's a screen time app for iOS and macOS that lets you choose your limits and how strict they should be.

I'm aware there are 999 competing screen time apps, but none worked quite right for us. So now there are 1000 competing screen time apps :)

It can range from just a short pause before opening a distracting app or website to needing a code from someone you've invited as an accountability partner.

It's free to get started and most of our friends/family are having good results using the free version daily so far.

Is anyone else finding themselves struggling to stay focused while waiting for coding agents to yield? What has helped you?

records.title: Show HN: RMBG – remove backgrounds from images in the browser (no uploads)
records.author: Velmet
records.storyText:
I am a person who does editing and digital designing. I used to use this tool, remove.bg, for getting transparent PNGs from either stock images or my own images. It was good, fast, free, and convenient. The only caveats for me were the export resolution limits and a privacy factor, that is, my images got uploaded to their servers.

Recently, remove.bg announced that they are shutting down the standalone website and moving to inside Canva only. This really made me sad. I have been using this tool for a long time now.

So, I made my own open-source tool, RMBG, which is: 1. Privacy-focused: the images never get uploaded somewhere; they stay and get processed only in your own browser. 2. No watermark or export resolution limits. 3. Fully free and open source with an MIT licence. No sign-in or accounts needed. 4. You can batch process and export as ZIP. 5. You can edit the image after the automated background removal, like erase objects, restore areas, recompute, etc. There are many view modes—mask, split, etc. 6. You can export in PNG, WebP, JPEG, and, in most browsers, AVIF. Other notes:

Behind the scenes, it uses the BiRefNet-lite AI model in ONNX through Transformers.js. Inference runs in a worker with WebGPU where available and a single-threaded WASM fallback.

The first visit downloads the runtime and about 98 MB of model weights from CDNs (that's why the first visit might be slower); later visits usually reuse the browser cache, so it can be fast.

There is minimal analytics, using only GoatCounter for small events such as page visits, successful inferences, and quality feedback. No image pixels, filenames, or dimensions are collected.

I am looking for contributors and as much help and support as possible, so I would appreciate people trying it out and giving feedback. Any ideas, PRs, and issues will be greatly appreciated.

I will be active on HN and will reply to comments here. Hope to see some support here!

Links: 1. Website - https://velmet44.github.io/rmbg/ 2. Source code on GitHub - https://github.com/Velmet44/rmbg 3. GoatCounter public analytics dashboard - https://velmet.goatcounter.com/ 4. Demo image - https://velmet44.github.io/rmbg/sample-split.png

records.title: Show HN: Global Compute, you pick. One API
records.author: anilj
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Anil.

I wanted to test the waters for a cloud computing site I created. It connects developers with access to the global compute using a unified API. It’s like a compute Marketplace.

You state what you need (region, price point, performance target) and deploy the same way, no matter which provider is underneath. I also benchmark every server and publish the results alongside per-second pricing.

Stack: The nodes that get created are basically Cloud Hypervisor VMMs on Ubuntu. I used Linux networking (VXLAN/NAT) to do all of the VPC and IP configs.

Disclaimer: This is early and the provider pool is small — mainly in Fremont, California (HE.net), and no other formal provider partnerships yet; I buy capacity the same way anyone would. That’s why some systems are reservable rather than instantly deployable.

Hoping for some feedback! I am very receptive to evolving this whole idea.

ps: There’s also $20 free compute credit for new users, if you want to poke at it.
